context:
Extract the skeleton (w1) before touching either adapter, so the interface
is designed against both existing implementations' actual needs rather
than generalized from just one. Resolve the casing question (w2) with a
grep across the codebase for table_stats consumers before choosing, since
this is the one place a wrong choice silently breaks a caller. Migrate
redshift and snowflake together in one PR (w3) so the drift is fixed
atomically rather than leaving one platform on the old pattern.
description:
Architecture review (Work Area E, structural remediation) found that
`benchbox/platforms/redshift.py:load_data` (starts at line 1794) and
`benchbox/platforms/snowflake.py:load_data` (starts at line 762)
independently implement the same staged-load orchestration loop - resolve
data files per table, upload/stage, run the platform load command, record
per-table row counts, log success/failure - with behavioral drift between
the two copies rather than a shared abstraction:

- Key casing: redshift keys `table_stats` by `table_name.lower()`
  (redshift.py:1817, 1828, 1838, 1849, 1859, 1870); snowflake keys by
  `table_name.upper()` (snowflake.py:791, 806, 816).
- Error reporting on failure: redshift logs the full error text
  (`error_message = str(e) or repr(e) or type(e).__name__`, then
  `self.logger.error(f"Failed to load {table_name}: {error_message}")`);
  snowflake truncates to `str(e)[:100]`
  (`self.logger.error(f"Failed to load {table_name}: {str(e)[:100]}...")`).
  Same failure class, different diagnostic fidelity depending on which
  platform hit it.

Similar near-identical duplication exists elsewhere in the same two files
plus databricks: `apply_unified_tuning` (redshift.py:2637 vs
snowflake.py:1748) and `close_connection`, which is actually triplicated
(redshift.py:2437, snowflake.py:1592,
`benchbox/platforms/databricks/adapter.py:2288`). This TODO focuses on the
staged-load loop first since it has observable behavioral drift (the key
casing difference could already be causing lookup bugs for any caller that
assumes a fixed case); the other duplications are cheaper copy-align fixes
once the load-loop template exists to model them on.

This is a targeted refactor, not a shrink-campaign item -
`_project/goal-shrink-core-code.md` explicitly scopes "dual-impl collapses
that trade correctness risk for lines" out of the autonomous shrink loop;
this work is done deliberately with adapter test coverage as the safety
net, not for line-count credit.

anti_patterns.dont: collapse apply_unified_tuning or close_connection into the same PR as the load-loop extraction
anti_patterns.why: each is a separate near-duplicate with its own risk surface; keep them as deferred follow-ups.

anti_patterns.dont: force bigquery/databricks onto the shared skeleton if their staging model does not actually match
anti_patterns.why: a forced-fit abstraction is worse than two adapters with an honest small duplication.

anti_patterns.dont: pick the casing convention without grepping downstream consumers of table_stats first
anti_patterns.why: a blind choice can silently break result reporting for whichever platform's casing changes.

deferrals.reason: Same duplication pattern as the load loop but a separate method; sequence after the staged-load template proves the extraction pattern works, to avoid landing two large simultaneous refactors in one PR.
deferrals.resolved_reason: [G4 sweep] duplicate: Deliberately sequenced follow-up under the same still-open staged-load-template item; not a separate untracked task. (tracked by cloud-adapter-staged-load-template)

deferrals.reason: Smaller and lower-risk than the load loop; a good follow-up once platforms/base has an established place for shared connection-lifecycle helpers (see benchbox/platforms/base/connection_lifecycle.py, which may already be the right home).
deferrals.resolved_reason: [G4 sweep] duplicate: Deferral is a note on its own from_item (cloud-adapter-staged-load-template), which is itself still open and planning this exact work.
deferrals.summary: Deduplicate the triplicated close_connection (redshift.py:2437, snowflake.py:1592, databricks/adapter.py:2288)

preserves.behavior: Existing result-capture and reporting code that reads table_stats keys continues to find its expected keys after the casing normalization in w2.
Per-platform load behavior (COPY vs PUT+COPY INTO, S3 staging vs Snowflake stage, file-format setup) verified by existing adapter tests continues to work identically after migration.
table_stats total row counts and the load_data return contract (tuple[dict[str, int], float, dict[str, Any] | None]) from benchbox/platforms/base/adapter.py:323 are unchanged.

prior_art.concept: benchbox/platforms/base/adapter.py:323 load_data abstract method - the existing contract both adapters implement; the new skeleton must satisfy this same signature/return contract.
benchbox/platforms/base/connection_lifecycle.py - likely existing home for the deferred close_connection deduplication; check before creating a new module for that follow-up.

benchbox/platforms/base/data_loading.py - existing shared data-loading helpers (COPY/CTAS loaders with trailing-delimiter handling per datafusion-tbl-trailing-delimiter-load) already used as a common base by other adapters; extend this file's pattern rather than starting a parallel shared-helpers module.

verifications.command: uv run -- python -m pytest tests -k 'redshift or snowflake' -m 'not slow and not stress' --tb=short
verifications.description: Redshift and Snowflake adapter load-data tests pass after migration to the shared skeleton
table_stats casing convention is consistent and documented
verifications.expected: both files use the same .lower() or .upper() convention on table_stats keys

work_units.notes:
Add a shared skeleton to `benchbox/platforms/base/data_loading.py` (or
a new `benchbox/platforms/base/staged_load.py` if data_loading.py is
already large) implementing: resolve data files via
`_resolve_data_files` -> per-table hook (upload/stage + platform-specific
load command, e.g. COPY/PUT+COPY INTO) -> collect stats -> aggregate
timing. The per-table load command and any platform-specific setup
(Redshift's S3 client + external schema, Snowflake's file formats +
query tag) stay as abstract hooks the subclass implements; only the
loop/bookkeeping/logging shape is shared.
work_units.summary: Extract a template-method staged-load skeleton in platforms/base

work_units.notes:
Pick one casing convention (lower or upper) for the shared skeleton's
`table_stats` dict keys. Check every caller of `load_data`'s returned
`table_stats` (result capture, reporting, validation) for any
case-sensitive lookup before picking, since changing either platform's
casing could silently break a caller that currently works only because
of that platform's specific case. Document the chosen convention in
the base class docstring so future adapters do not reintroduce drift.
work_units.summary: Normalize table_stats key casing and document the choice

work_units.notes:
Reimplement `RedshiftAdapter.load_data` and `SnowflakeAdapter.load_data`
as thin per-table hooks over the new base skeleton, removing the
duplicated loop/logging code. Normalize the error-logging behavior to
one policy (recommend: log full error text like redshift currently
does, since truncating to 100 chars as snowflake does can hide the
actionable part of a load error) - state the choice and rationale in
the PR body.
work_units.summary: Migrate redshift.py and snowflake.py to the shared skeleton

work_units.notes:
After redshift+snowflake prove the template out, check whether
`benchbox/platforms/bigquery.py` and
`benchbox/platforms/databricks/adapter.py` have a load_data loop
similar enough to migrate, or whether their staging model (e.g.
Databricks' different ingestion path) genuinely differs enough that
forcing them onto the same skeleton would hurt readability. Migrate
only if it is a clean fit; otherwise record why they are excluded.
work_units.summary: Evaluate bigquery/databricks for the same template
